analysis.one_liner: Lets employers count more of tipped workers' tips toward the minimum wage they owe.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee and died when the 101st Congress ended, after drawing only three cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Under federal law, employers of tipped workers can count a share of each worker's tips toward the minimum wage they are required to pay, so the worker's guaranteed cash wage from the employer is the minimum wage minus that credit. This bill would raise that share from 40% of the minimum wage to 45% in 1989 and 50% from 1990 onward. That means employers — mostly restaurants — would pay less cash out of pocket, and workers would depend more on customer tips for their base pay.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers of tipped workers, chiefly restaurants, would gain: every dollar of tips above the higher credit would no longer count toward their minimum-wage liability, so their required cash payroll would fall for every tipped employee [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Raises the cap on how much of a tipped worker's tips an employer can credit against the minimum wage from 40% to 45% in 1989 and 50% thereafter [S2][S3].
Because the credit comes out of the employer's minimum-wage liability, the increase directly reduces the cash wage employers must guarantee to tipped employees [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Tipped workers would bear the cost: as the credit rose to half the minimum wage, the guaranteed cash pay from their employer would fall, leaving their income more dependent on customer tips, which vary with business conditions and are not guaranteed [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill raises the tip credit from 40% to 45% and then 50%, so an employer could satisfy half of the minimum wage obligation with customer tips instead of cash pay [S2][S3].

Tips are not guaranteed: they fluctuate with customer traffic and discretion, so shifting more of the wage floor onto tips leaves workers' base income less secure and harder to predict — a cost an honest supporter would have to acknowledge.
The bill contains no offsetting provision for workers — no change to the minimum wage itself, no tip-pooling protection, nothing that raises any tipped employee's guaranteed pay [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's entire effect is to shift part of the minimum-wage obligation from employers onto workers' tip earnings, lowering employers' cash labor costs during the minimum-wage increases of the era while reducing the guaranteed portion of tipped workers' pay. There is no gain to workers anywhere in the bill, and the cost falls on some of the lowest-paid employees in the workforce.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee, which asked the Labor Department for its comments but never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Sen. Tom Harkin introduced the bill on January 25, 1989, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources [S1][S5].
On February 14, 1989, the committee requested executive comment from the Department of Labor — the last action the bill ever received [S5].
The bill attracted only three cosponsors — two Senate Republicans and one Senate Democrat — and never reached the Senate floor or a committee vote before the 101st Congress ended [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tipped workers are better off because the bill died: the cap on how much of their tips employers could count toward the minimum wage stayed at 40%, so employers could not cut their guaranteed cash pay the way the bill would have allowed. Restaurant and other tipped-service employers lost the chance to lower that obligation.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Tipped workers, who kept the 40% cap

for.name: Tom Harkin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to raise the tip credit and referred it to the Labor and Human Resources Committee.

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.what_they_did: Received the bill, requested executive comment from the Department of Labor on February 14, 1989, and then took no further action; the bill never got a markup or a floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll calls exist; its sponsorship was bipartisan but tiny — one Democratic sponsor, one Democratic cosponsor, and two Republican cosponsors.

industries.note: Restaurants employ most tipped workers, so the higher 45% and 50% tip credit would cut the guaranteed cash wage they must pay each tipped employee. The industry's gain comes directly out of workers' guaranteed pay, since customers' tips would cover half the minimum wage obligation.
Any employer covered by the Fair Labor Standards Act's tipped-employee rules could count more tips toward the minimum wage, lowering required cash payroll at the expense of workers' guaranteed pay.
